Title: Study of Thermal Conductivity and Reliability of InAg Soldering Thermal Interface Material by Formic Acid Reflow for TIM1 IC Module Package

Thermal Interface Material by Formic Acid Reflow for TIM1 IC 
Module Package

Abstract 
Indium and indium-containing alloys such as indium silver (InAg) alloys have generally been paid 
considerable attention as thermal interface materials for usage in thermal management of microprocessors 
such as CPU, GPU and AI accelerator. This is, especially true for high-performance computing electronics 
with high power density. Reflow process parameters of InAg preforms with differing compositions of Ag 
ranging from 3 to 10 wt% as well as various thicknesses were extensively studied bonding Cu to Cu to 
achieve optimum properties and performance of the InAg soldered joint using formic acid vacuum reflow. 
Basic characterization was also completed including basic physical properties such as density, modulus and 
phase transition. Moreover, X-ray scanning and confocal scanning acoustic microscopy (C-SAM) were used 
to identify voids and delamination of the InAg soldered joints, respectively. Laser Flash Analysis (LFA) was 
employed to measure thermal conductivity of the soldered joint bonding Cu to Cu after the reflow process in 
the determined optimum conditions. Thermal cycling testing (TCT) was conducted with a profile of -40°C 
to 125°C, 30 min of dwell time and highly accelerated stress testing (HAST) with a profile of 
110°C/85%RH/0.22 MPa/264 hr, to evaluate reliability of the soldered joints, the initial characterization 
testing was repeated at several intervals. To further understand the change of microstructure after the given 
number of thermal cycling, cross-sectional samples were prepared and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) 
was used to characterize morphologies of the soldered joints. In this presentation, the influence of the 
different compositions of InAg alloys and bond line thickness (BLT) on the voiding performance, 
delamination and thermal conductivity of the soldered joints, as well as the results of reliability are discussed.   
 
Key words 
Vacuum reflow, Reliability, Preform, voiding, Indium Silver 
 
 
 
I. Introduction 
In current electronic packaging a processor die generates 
heat during operation. A thermal interface material (TIM) 1 
is used to help conduct the heat between a processor die and 
heat-spreader. A TIM 2 then conducts heat between the heat-
spreader and the heatsink [1]. As devices continue to trend 
towards smaller size and higher frequency, integration, 
power, and speed the need for high performance TIMs is 
greater than ever [2,3,4]. There are several types of TIMs, 
this includes greases, gels, liquid metals, phase change 
materials (PCMs), solders and thermal adhesives [5]. Many 
of these including greases, gels, PCMs and thermal adhesives 
are generally polymer based. While improvements have been 
made recently, polymer based TIMs often have low thermal 
conductivities and high thermal contact resistance [6]. While 
polymer based TIMs have been popular in the past, the 
growing need for high performance has led to the rise of 
metal based TIMs. These have several benefits such as high 
durability and better thermal properties than polymer-based 
materials without the worry of outgassing and residue [7]. 
This project focused entirely on solder thermal interface 
materials (sTIMs) being used as a TIM 1. Solder TIMs have 
the benefit of a high bulk thermal conductivity and low 
thermal resistance after soldering. While pure indium is a 
fantastic thermal transfer material [8], voiding can be an 
issue and is caused by trapped air and gases produced with 
the use of flux within the system. With the addition of silver, 
the thermal conductivity is increased while also adding to 
reliability strength. In this study, the focus was placed on 
determining a method for flux-less reflow of sTIMs using a 
formic acid vacuum reflow oven.

II. Experiment and Characterization 
A. Materials 
Indium silver (InAg) preforms were produced internally with 
Indium Corporation. Punched copper disks were used for the 
substrate and lid with the InAg sandwiched between. Both 
the preforms and copper disks were about 1” in diameter. 
B. Characterization 
B1. Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) 
A DSC was used to determine the endo and exothermic peaks 
for each preform composition to determine the solidus and 
liquidus ranges. The test was comprised of two heating and 
cooling cycles. From 40°C to 300°C at 20°C/min then 300°C 
to 40°C at -20°C/min. 
 
B2. Reflow and profiling 
For all reflow and profiling, a formic acid vacuum reflow 
oven was used.  
 
B3. Imaging 
After reflow was completed, voiding was measured using an 
X-ray. Delamination was checked for using confocal 
scanning acoustic microscopy (C-SAM). 
 
B4. Reliability 
Two different reliability tests were used throughout the 
experiment. Thermal cycling testing (TCT) was used after 
reflow and was set for -40°C to 125°C with a 30-minute 
dwell time. The total cycle time was about 100 minutes. The 
samples were removed and checked at 100, 250, 500 and 
1000 cycles. A highly accelerated stress test (HAST) 
chamber was used and set to 85% relative humidity (RH) and 
110°C for 264 hours. The samples were checked at 24, 72, 
168, and 264 hours.  
 
B5. Thermal Conductivity Measurement 
After reflow the sandwiched samples, Cu-InAg-Cu, were 
tested using laser flash analysis. Samples were measured 
post-reflow, then at several intervals throughout TCT and 
HAST.  
 
III. Results and Discussion 
The first focus was on obtaining the material properties of 
the alloy preforms to find any trends as Ag wt.% increases. 
Using DSC, the endo and exothermic peaks were found to 
determine melting and freezing points. The results of the 
DSC runs are shown in Table I.  
As seen in the DSC trials, as the percent Ag increases, the 
liquidus temp increases further from the eutectic point [9]. 
The 97/03 composition is near eutectic for this system. Using 
the data from the DSC the general reflow conditions were 
chosen. The process was completed flux-less and instead 
formic acid was used to remove the indium surface oxide. 
Formic acids activation range is 160-200°C. Starting around 
160°C the formic acid reacts with the metal oxide to form a 
formate salt. Then as the temperature approaches 200°C the 
formate breaks down leaving an unoxidized surface [10, 11]. 
With this in mind 90/10 InAg was selected for its higher 
liquidus point giving more time for the oxide to be removed. 
Reflow samples were composed of a 1” diameter InAg 
preform between two 1” diameter Cu coupons. Testing 
comprised of different melt temperatures, formic acid soak 
times, and time under vacuum. The samples were then 
qualified through void analysis by both X-ray and c-SAM. 
Keeping the activation temperature of formic acid and the 
preform DSC data in mind, peak reflow temperatures of 
180°C to 290°C were investigated. The subsequent profiling 
data is shown in Table II.

Throughout reflow testing it was observed that as peak 
reflow temperature was decreased closer to the formic acid 
activation temperature, 180°C, the quality of the joint formed 
decreased in terms of voiding. This was especially evident 
while testing 97/03 InAg. At lower peak temps, about 25°C 
above the liquidus, no strong joint was able to be formed. 
This is likely due to the formate not fully decomposing. 
During testing, reflow temperatures below 240°C showed 
substantially higher voiding (15.09%) than higher reflow 
temperatures (1.90%). Thickness of the preform had the 
largest effect on joint performance. Initial results showed 
that increasing thickness helps the reflow process. This is due 
to the ease of handling, the thinner the preform the more 
likely deformation is to occur during part placement. Defects 
generated through handling the preforms then transferred to 
the joint. It was observed that defects such as bent edges or 
scratches would carry-over throughout the reflow process.

The thinner preforms were more malleable causing more 
defects. A vacuum pen was used to limit this to an extent. 
Fig. 1 shows an example of voiding results between two 
different thicknesses.

Fig. 1: X-ray comparison between 4 and 8 mil InAg 
preforms post-reflow.  
 
Another factor in the reflow processing conditions is the 
effect of the vacuum during reflow. As seen in Fig. 1, the 
thinner 4 mil preform has large voiding at the edges. The 
thicker preforms show much less or no edge voiding. The 
vacuum aids in drawing out the voids. During profiling 
testing, the vacuum was run ranging from no vacuum to three 
minutes at 5 mBar. The final profile-initiated vacuum after 
reaching the liquidus temperature and held for 60 seconds. 
The profile used for reliability is shown in Fig. 2. 
 
 
Fig. 2: Profile used for reliability samples. The vacuum is 
held for 60 seconds once above liquidus temperature. 
Time above liquidus is 180 s, peak temp is 270°C. 
 
The effect of the vacuum on thinner preforms was small 
leaving large edge voids while limiting them with the thicker 
ones. This is likely due to thicker preforms having more 
material to “pull” filling the edge voids. Because of these 
factors it was decided to continue the reliability tests with the 
90/10 InAg 8 mil preforms. Samples post-reflow had initial 
voiding and thermal conductivity data measured. Voiding 
was quantified through both X-ray and C-SAM while 
thermal conductivity was determined through laser flash 
analysis. Reliability samples underwent both TCT and 
HAST chamber testing with samples undergoing both 
measurements again at several intervals. Fig. 3 is the thermal 
conductivity throughout HAST. The samples were removed, 
tested and then placed back into the chamber. 
 
 
Fig. 3: Thermal conductivity results post-HAST testing 
by laser flash analysis. A decrease of 4.3 W/(m∙K) is seen 
from time zero to 264 hours. 
 
Fig. 4 includes the HAST voiding data. Both Fig. 3 and 4 
show the same trend. The samples have an initial increase in 
voiding % and decrease in thermal conductivity. From 168 
hours on the results plateau and no major change is seen. 
 
 
Fig. 4: Voiding results post-HAST by X-ray and C-SAM. 
An increase of 2.39 voiding % was measured from time 
zero to 264 hours. 
 
Overall, the HAST samples performed well, demonstrating 
the ability to maintain a relatively high thermal conductivity 
around 45 (W/m∙K) throughout 11 days or 264 hours of 
HAST testing. The void analysis data also follows a similar 
trend with voiding slowly increasing and plateauing around 
5.72%.

A second batch of reliability samples were produced for TCT 
and measured at several intervals. Fig. 5 includes the initial 
TCT thermal conductivity results. 
 
 
Fig. 5: Thermal conductivity results post-TCT testing. 
After 1000 cycles an average decrease of 1.77 (W/m∙K) 
was measured. 
 
These same samples were also tested for voiding at each 
stage. The averaged results of both X-ray and C-SAM are 
shown in Fig. 6. 
 
Fig. 6: Voiding results post-TCT by X-ray and C-SAM. 
After 1000 cycles an increase of 1.97 voiding % was 
measured. 
 
The results from Fig. 4 and 6 mimic each other. Both 
reliability tests show an initial increase, with voiding 
plateauing for the final 2 intervals. Images of this void data 
is shown in both Tables III and IV. 
 
After HAST the samples increased in voiding but it was not 
a significant increase (2.39%). Samples starting with larger 
edge voids ended with the largest void growth. Likely due to 
the high amount of moisture and pressure on the joint 
throughout testing. The TCT void data looked similar to 
these results as well. The TCT void results are shown in 
Table IV. 
 
The TCT results were similar to what was seen in the HAST. 
The voiding was more inconsistent with a higher standard 
deviation for multiple test intervals, but low percent voiding 
and thermal conductivity stability was observed throughout.

III. Conclusion 
Testing has shown the ability for soldered thermal interface 
material to reflow flux-less in a vacuum oven with formic 
acid while maintaining a relatively high thermal conductivity 
and low voiding. This study focused on the processing and 
reliability of InAg preforms with different compositions and 
thicknesses. It was found that the preform thickness plays an 
important role on the voiding performance, the thicker 
preforms provided better voiding. The test coupons showed 
good reliability under harsh HAST and TCT conditions. No 
obvious degradation of thermal conductivity was observed 
after HAST and TCT. Meanwhile, there was only a slight, 
2.39%, increase in voiding. Compared to the standard flux-
based process, there is no flux residue in the joint/assembly 
after processing by vacuum reflow with formic acid.

Abstract: Indium and indium-containing alloys such as indium silver (InAg) alloys have generally been paid considerable attention as thermal interface materials for usage in thermal management of microprocessors such as CPU, GPU and AI accelerator. This is, especially true for high-performance computing electronics with high power density. Reflow process parameters of InAg preforms with differing compositions of Ag ranging from 3 to 10 wt% as well as various thicknesses were extensively studied bonding Cu to Cu to achieve optimum properties and performance of the InAg soldered joint using formic acid vacuum reflow. Basic characterization was also completed including basic physical properties such as density, modulus and phase transition. Moreover, X-ray scanning and confocal scanning acoustic microscopy (C-SAM) were used to identify voids and delamination of the InAg soldered joints, respectively. Laser Flash Analysis (LFA) was employed to measure thermal conductivity of the soldered joint bonding Cu to Cu after the reflow process in the determined optimum conditions. Thermal cycling testing (TCT) was conducted with a profile of -40°C to 125°C, 30 min of dwell time and highly accelerated stress testing (HAST) with a profile of 110°C/85%RH/0.22 MPa/264 hr, to evaluate reliability of the soldered joints, the initial characterization testing was repeated at several intervals. To further understand the change of microstructure after the given number of thermal cycling, cross-sectional samples were prepared and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to characterize morphologies of the soldered joints. In this presentation, the influence of the different compositions of InAg alloys and bond line thickness (BLT) on the voiding performance, delamination and thermal conductivity of the soldered joints, as well as the results of reliability are discussed.
